title: Unless the Lord build (Psalm 126 [127])
hookLine: they labor in vain that build without him

cards: It's eleven at night. The laptop is still open. One more email, one more fix, one more thing, and you tell yourself if you push a little longer, it'll all hold together.
The coffee's cold. Tomorrow you'll get up early and do it again. It's the loop where everything seems to rest on one person, and stopping for a second feels like letting it all fall down.
Long ago, someone wrote a psalm for exactly that person.

teach.b: Another of the gradual psalms, and the heading gives it to Solomon, the king who built the Temple. It opens with two pictures.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." First, what it doesn't say.
It doesn't say don't build, or fire the watchman. The builder still lays bricks; the guard still stands on the wall. The psalm is about who the work finally rests on.
Second, the tired worker. The next verse calls it vain to rise before light, eating the bread of sorrow.
Then a line of real gentleness: "When he shall give sleep to his beloved." In the psalm, rest isn't laziness. It's trust: the house isn't held up by one pair of hands.
In Hebrew, house can mean a building and also a family, a household, a line of children.

teach.h: UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.
teach.b: So the psalm goes on to children as a gift from the Lord. Build a home, raise a family, run a city: the psalm says all of it rests on God first.
The Latin opening, Nisi Dominus, was set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi, and it's carved as a motto over doors and on city arms.
Catholics also have an old habit that fits it well: the morning offering, a prayer at the start of the day that hands over all the day's work before it begins.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 126 [127] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some begin the day with a morning offering, a traditional prayer that offers the day's work, joys and sufferings to God.

s: the psalm tells people to stop working
the builder still builds and the watchman still watches. it's about who the work finally rests on.
in Hebrew, house can also mean a family
that's why the psalm goes on to speak of children as a gift from the Lord.
the psalm treats sleep as a gift
"when he shall give sleep to his beloved."

games.q: it's late, the work isn't finished, and you feel the whole house depends on you. what does the psalm point to?
o: stay up all night and finish it.
trust the Lord with the house, and sleep.
games.why: it calls rising before light to eat the bread of sorrow vain, and speaks of the Lord "when he shall give sleep to his beloved."

practice: Name the main thing you'll work on today, a project, a shift, homework, looking after someone, and see yourself starting it.

If you pray, hand it over: this is yours, Lord, before it's mine; some Catholics use the morning offering for this. If you don't pray, set an intention: I'll do my part, and I won't carry the whole house alone.

wordCard.voice: Nisi Dominus. Latin for unless the Lord, the first words of a psalm that says our work, our cities and our families rest on God, not on our effort alone. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: unless the Lord, the psalm's first words in the Vulgate, set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi.

carryVoice: Your line: not in vain. In this psalm, even sleep is a gift. One hundred eighty-six days in.
